Hangsik Shin∗ and Chungkeun Lee
Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Y onsei University , Seoul, Korea
Autonomic nervous system (ANS) has been assessed by heart rate variability (HRV) based on beat-to beat
interval of electrocardiogram (ECG). In this paper,as a surrogate method of the HRV , weinvestigate pulse rate
variability (PRV) based on a non-invasive blood volume change measurement technique, photoplethysmography
(PPG). ANS activity is speculated with vessel characteristicssuch as vaso-activities induced by sympathetic or
parasympathetic nervous system. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) index is used to investigate these vaso-activities.
PPG is measured from both ﬁngertip and toe to investigate the physiological differences by measuring site. From
the experimental results, it was conﬁrmed that the signiﬁcance of assessment fromPRV is evenly matched with
HRV in SDNN, pNN50 and HF analysis. The result of this paper suggests that the PRV could be a surrogate
method in ANS assessment instead of HRV in speciﬁed condition.
Keywords: Autonomic Nervous System (ANS), Heart Rate Variability (HRV), Pulse Rate Variability (PRV),
Pulse Wave Velocity (PWV), Photoplethysmography (PPG).

1. INTRODUCTION
The autonomic nervous system (ANS), the part of the peripheral
nervous system that acts as a control system functioning largely
below the level of consciousness and controls internal functions,
is classically divided into two subsystems: the parasympathetic
nervous system and sympathetic nervous system. ANS is respon-
sible for up- and down-regulating several homeostatic mecha-
nisms such as heart rate, respiration, vaso-constriction/dilation,
pupil diameter, gut motility, and urinary output. The term of
ﬁght-or-ﬂight response and rest-and-digest response have been
used to describe the functional mediation of the neuronal and
hormonal stress response. Fight-or-ﬂight response corresponds
with arousal and energy generation and inhibits digestion, and
it is promoted by sympathetic nervous system. Rest-and-digest
response expedites calming of the nerves return to regular func-
tion and enhances digestion, and it is promoted by parasympa-
thetic nervous system.
In ANSassessment, heart rate variability (HRV) has inten-
sively investigated. The power spectrum of HRV is known as
an assessment index of the sympathetic, parasympathetic activ-
ity and sympathovagal balance. HRV has been investigated with
very low frequency (VLF), low frequency (LF) and high fre-
quency(HF) components over 0.0033–0.04 Hz, 0.04–0.15 Hz and

0.15–0.4 Hz, respectively. It is a general opinion that LF compo-
nents are attributed to the activities of sympathetic and parasym-
pathetic nervous system and HF components are mediated by the
parasympathetic nervous system. Moreover, the ratio of low- to
high-frequency power (LF/HF) is known as the index of sympa-
thovagal balances.
In recent study, there are many researches of PRV based on
PPG signal as a noninvasive surrogate method for HRV . PPG
is measured by skin contact-based optical sensor and it reﬂects
blood volume changes at a speciﬁed spot such as ﬁngertip, toe,
forehead and ear. It has already been demonstrated that the pulse
to pulse interval (PPI) derived from PPG could be a surrogate
R to R interval (RRI) of ECG by several researches. However,
though PPI has a similar characteristic to RRI, PPI should be
affected by hemodynamic characteristics, and it could be a reason
of the difference between HRV and PRV . For example, PRV does
not precisely reﬂect HRV in controlled conditions such as posture
changing or cardiac pacing. Moreover, it was validated by the
investigations of PPG baseline and amplitude that PPG contains
spontaneous ﬂuctuations and these ﬂuctuations are mediated by
autonomic nervous system. These characteristics provide rather
the possibilities for the novel assessment method of ANS than
the evidence that PRV is not deserved to use for assessment of
ANS. In previous researches, it was suggested that the LF waves
in ﬁnger PPG could be a sensitive marker of sympathetic activity
for the peripheral circulation.

PPG has been measured from several peripheral sites. There-
fore, PRV could be also derived from multi-site measured PPG.
Different waveforms were found from the different measuring
sites, because each site includes own angiological and vascular
characteristics. Moreover, different path length and site could be
a reason of deformation of PPG waveform. High correlation was
found between ﬁnger-PPG and toe-PPG, and this result implies
that PPI or PRV may have minor differences by measuring site.
Although HRV is possible to represent an effective concep-
tual framework for a practical and common preclinical tool of
cardiovascular neural regulation, there are many debates of the
clinical reproducibility. Therefore, to investigate the PRV as a
surrogate method for ANS assessment, we not only compared
PRV with HRV , but also compared with PWV index which could
thoroughly reﬂect autonomic vascular activity and hemodynamic
properties. It was well-known fact that PWV is the standard
method in measuring arterial stiffness or distensibility. Moreover,
there were several reports referred that arterial distensibility is
closely related with ANS activity, and that sympathetic overac-
tivity may be the contributor of reduced arterial distensibility
observed in patients with essential hypertension based on spec-
trum analysis of HRV . In this paper, PWV indices, closely esti-
mated PWV which calculated with pulse transit time (PTT) and
measuring distance, were used for ANS assessment as a sur-
rogate index of PWV . We postulated that PRV which involves
hemodynamic properties could be more suitable than HRV which
dominantly controlled by central nervous system for arterial
distensibility-based ANS activity assessment.
The present study aims to compare the ANS activity derived
by HRV and PRV , and to investigate the PRV as a surrogate

method of ANSassessment. Our study was designed to (1) derive
HRV and PRV , (2) compare PRV with HRV by PWV index, and
(3) assess whether PRV can help to identify autonomic activity
with experimental data.
2. METHOD
2.1. Heart Rate Variability
HRV was derived by beat-to-beat intervals analysis from the mea-
sured RRI of ECG, and was analyzed by time- and frequency-
analysis method to assess ANS activity. Two time domain
analytic methods were used in HRV analysis:
(1) SDNN (standard deviation of normal RRI) reﬂects long-term
variability or LF power and
(2) pNN50 (percent of difference between adjacent normal RRI
that are greater than 50 ms) reﬂects mainly vagal tone or HF
power.
For frequency domain analysis, power spectrum was calculated
by non-parametric method, Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). LF,
HF, and LF/HF were calculated and compared for assessment
of sympathetic activity. Preprocessing was performed for HRV
measurement: interpolation, re-sampling, linear trends removal,
and windowing. Interpolation was carried out for RRI regula-
tion because RRI index has non-uniform time intervals and it is
not proper to spectrum analysis. Therefore, spline interpolation
(1 kHz) and re-sampling (7 Hz) was successively performed in
order to regulate RRI. Linear trends removal and Hanning win-
dowing was also carried before spectrum analysis.

2.2. Pulse Rate Variability
PRV was calculated by beat-to-beat intervals analysis from the
measured PPI from PPG. Both cases of PRV were analyzed with
ﬁnger-PPG(PPGf ) and toe-PPG(PPG t/rparenorisignal. Each PRV was
derived and analyzed by identical time- and frequency-analysis
method of HRV analysis to compare with HRV .
2.3. Pulse Wave Velocity Indices
Doppler ﬂow metry technology enables to measure the PWV
exactly, but it needs additional apparatus besides ECG and PPG
measurement devices. Because we designed the simple approach
to estimate the PWV indirectly, PWV index is calculated with the
PTT and the superﬁcial length between measuring sites. Super-
ﬁcial length might not reﬂect exact vessel structures and length,
in other words, natural error should be included in estimated
PWV indices. In other words, PWV index is an approximated
parameter to estimate PWV because it was based on not only
approximated vessel length, but also time duration hybridized of
electrical and physical physiological signal. Therefore, estimated
PWV indices might have some errors compared with real value
of PWV .

2.4. Experimental Method
Twenty three subjects (11 male and 12 female, mean ages of 22.1
years, range 19–29 years) were participated in experiment. The
study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board
and adhered to the declaration of Helsinki. Prior to the experi-
ment, all subjects were requested to provide information about
their physical condition and none reported any taking medicine
or signs of cardiovascular or respiratory disease. For reliable sta-
tistical analysis, dataset was normalized by quantile–quantile plot
(QQ-plot), and reconstruct the dataset with 14 subjects (6 male
and 8 female, mean ages of 21.2 years, range 19–24 years). Nor-
malized QQ-plots are shown in Figure 2. Physical information
such as height, weight and BMI were also measured for demo-
graphical research and summarized in Table I. Every experiment
was performed in a typical sports medicine laboratory at an ambi-
ent room temperature from 11 am to 6 pm. Drinking and smoking
were prohibited during 24 hour and 2 hour before experiment,
respectively.
ECG and PPG were simultaneously recorded by MP150
(Biopacinc., USA) and supplement modules. ECG was recorded
on the chest surface with LEAD II conﬁguration, and PPG was
measured on left index ﬁnger with TSD100B, plethysmography
transducer. MA TLAB 2008b (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA,
